name: AMF bed nets, wellbeing analysis
beneficiaries_note: Nothing in the model says where; the charity's main country of operation, the one its other models name most: Democratic Republic of the Congo.

missing_data.note: Measured: AMF counts the nets distributed, and the effect is from randomised trials of the same nets.

summary: Distributes insecticide-treated bed nets to protect people from malaria. The Happier Lives Institute's analysis of AMF in wellbeing terms (WELLBYs). Its result depends heavily on a philosophical choice HLI leaves open: the neutral point above which a life counts as good. HLI found AMF less cost-effective than StrongMinds under almost all views it considered.

source.title: The elephant in the bednet: the importance of philosophy when choosing between extending and improving lives

sections.title: Value of the lives saved
sections.explainer: Deaths averted, each worth the wellbeing of the years saved, plus grief averted for the family.

sections.title: Discounting
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, not HLI's: HLI counts wellbeing the same whenever it comes. Our view discounts the life-improving benefits at the discount rate under Your values; the evaluator view pins it at 0. Deaths averted now are valued as a whole and not discounted.

rows.label: Deaths averted per $1,000, before leverage and funging (GiveWell's AMF model)

source.title: GiveWell, AMF cost-effectiveness analysis (September 2026)
source.note: 196.04 lives counterfactually saved per $1m (after GiveWell's supplemental adjustments and its −15.49% leverage and funging adjustment), divided back by (1 − 0.1549) to 231.97 per $1m before leverage and funging. HLI's 0.3353 per $1,000 is GiveWell's 2022 figure per dollar AMF spends, before those adjustments (HLI sheet, 'GiveWell Numbers'!B8).

rows.explainer: Changed for consistency: our view takes the deaths from GiveWell's current AMF model, the other model of this charity on the site, so both count the same deaths. HLI used its copy of GiveWell's 2022 model, 0.335 per $1,000 per dollar AMF spends, before GiveWell's leverage and funging adjustment (kept in the evaluator view). GiveWell's adjustment for leverage and funging follows below, under the same switch as in GiveWell's model.

rows.label: GiveWell's adjustment for leverage and funging

source.title: GiveWell, AMF cost-effectiveness analysis (September 2026)
source.note: 'Leverage and funging adjustment for counterfactual outcome estimates', −15.49%.

rows.explainer: Changed for consistency: GiveWell's own adjustment for money the grant pulls in from others (leverage) or pushes away (funging), as its AMF model applies it to lives saved. With credit by share of resources on, it is 0 and AMF gets its share of the whole campaign instead, as in GiveWell's model. HLI applied none (0 in the evaluator view).

rows.label: Deaths averted per $1,000, counted
Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five

source.title: GiveWell, AMF cost-effectiveness analysis (September 2026)
source.note: 202.57 under-five deaths of 250.66 averted per $1m, before adjustments.

rows.explainer: From GiveWell's current AMF model, whose deaths our view counts: about 81% are children under five, the rest people five and older. (HLI's 2022 copy put the average age at 20.)

rows.label: Weight on HLI's own value of a life saved (evaluator view only)
rows.explainer: Changed for consistency: 0 in our view, so HLI's own value of a life saved drops out and every death counts at the site's value (Discounting); 1 in the evaluator view, so HLI's own figure, with its neutral point, reproduces. A switch between the two, not a blend.

rows.label: Average age of those saved
rows.explainer: Deaths averted weighted between under-fives (average age 1.5) and over-fives (46.1).

rows.label: Life expectancy used
rows.explainer: Average life expectancy in AMF's countries, from GiveWell's model.

rows.label: Years of life saved per death averted
Average life satisfaction in AMF's countries (0–10)
rows.explainer: From the Gallup World Poll, as used by HLI.

rows.label: Neutral point on the 0–10 life-satisfaction scale
rows.explainer: The level of life satisfaction at which life is neither good nor bad for the person living it. Below it, extra years count as bad; above it, good. HLI shows results for 0 to 5 and picks none; the best guess of 2 is ours, close to the value some survey respondents report. This single choice moves AMF's result more than any other input.

rows.label: Life satisfaction above the neutral point
WELLBYs from the years of life saved
Yearly rise in life satisfaction over time
rows.explainer: Life satisfaction in these countries has been rising; later years of a life saved are expected to be better.

rows.label: WELLBYs from rising life satisfaction
Effect of a child's death on a family member's life satisfaction
rows.explainer: From Oswald and Powdthavee, via HLI.

rows.label: Years the grief lasts
rows.explainer: HLI's estimate of how long the effect of bereavement lasts.

rows.label: Other household members
rows.explainer: Average household size in AMF's countries minus one, from GiveWell's model.

rows.label: WELLBYs from grief averted
WELLBYs per life saved (HLI)
rows.explainer: HLI's value of a life saved: the wellbeing of the years the person goes on to live above the neutral point, rising over time, plus grief averted for the family. The evaluator view uses it; our view values deaths the site's way (below).

rows.label: WELLBYs from saving lives per $1,000
rows.explainer: HLI's WELLBYs from the lives saved. Our view counts the deaths outside this row (0 here, see Discounting): valued the site's way, not by HLI's WELLBYs of the years lived above a neutral point.

rows.label: WELLBYs from better health and income per $1,000
rows.explainer: Less malaria illness and higher later incomes, including community spillovers at 75% net coverage. HLI publishes two cases: its 'just life saving' version, which leaves these out (0), and its upper bound, 29.97 (its lower-bound tab is broken in the published sheet, #REF!). Changed for consistency: like everywhere else on the site our view takes a central figure, here the middle of HLI's two cases, 15.0, with the two as the range; HLI's sheet adds its upper bound (kept in the evaluator view).

rows.label: WELLBYs per $1,000
Discount rate on future wellbeing
rows.explainer: The shared discount rate (Your values). HLI doesn't discount, so the evaluator view pins it at 0.

rows.label: Years from the nets until the life-improving benefit starts, on average
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Part of the benefit is less malaria while the nets last (the first two to three years), part is higher incomes when the children protected grow up (GiveWell counts these from about ten years on). One start year, 3, stands in for the mix; 0 is all illness, 10 all income.

rows.label: Years the life-improving benefit is spread over
rows.explainer: Our judgment: from three years (illness only, the life of a net) to forty (GiveWell's working life for the income gains), with 20 for the mix.

rows.label: Discount factor for the life-improving benefit
rows.explainer: The WELLBYs spread evenly over those years from the start year, discounted to today, as a share of their undiscounted total: 1 at a 0% rate.

rows.label: Value of averting a death, by age (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights, as in its AMF model: 116.25 doubled-income years for a child under five, 73.19 for a person five or older, times "A child's life vs doubled-income year" (Your values).

rows.label: Value of the deaths averted per $1,000, the site's way (units of value)
rows.explainer: Changed for consistency: in our view a death averted is valued the way every model on the site values it, GiveWell's moral weight for the age of the person saved (facts: moral_weights) times "A child's life vs doubled-income year" (Your values), not by HLI's WELLBYs of the years the person goes on to live above a neutral point. 0 in the evaluator view, where HLI's own value counts. Deaths averted now are not discounted. Grief averted for the family is part of what a death costs and is not added on top, as in GiveWell's models.

rows.label: WELLBYs per $1,000 from the deaths averted
rows.explainer: The deaths' value in units of value (above), put into WELLBYs at the WELLBY rate ("1 point more life satisfaction for a year vs doubled-income year", Your values). The unit's conversion multiplies every WELLBY by the same rate, so the two cancel: the deaths count their shared value whatever the WELLBY slider says, and only the WELLBYs HLI measured move with it. The one row a model may read the WELLBY rate in (docs/normalization.md 2.3, INV-17).

rows.label: WELLBYs per $1,000, discounted
AMF's share of all spending on its net campaigns
rows.explainer: HLI's deaths averted per $1,000 come from GiveWell's figures per dollar AMF spends. Governments pay the rest of the campaign cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, AMF gets only its share. Best guess is GiveWell's DRC figure; the range spans its other locations.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of program cost
rows.explainer: Default for programs that mostly buy and hand out goods (nets, drugs, supplements, vaccines, water treatment): staff pay is a small part of the cost. Our judgment; we haven't seen this program's breakdown.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: Delivery staff are mostly hired locally at local rates, so the gap is small. Our judgment.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff per dollar of cost (in-kind donation)
Share of the full cost paid in cash
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, staff's forgone pay counts as part of the cost, and staff get their share of the outcome. Off, this is 100%.

rows.label: WELLBYs per dollar
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, times AMF's share of all spending and the share of the full cost paid in cash (staff's forgone pay is the rest).
